title: Data Visualization (Matplotlib & Seaborn)
description: 2D Matplotlib plots, subplots, line charts, figure styling, and statistical distribution analysis with Seaborn.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Figure, Line Plots & Subplots
lessons.concept_markdown:
- **Anatomy**: A Matplotlib `Figure` contains one or more `Axes` (the plotting canvas). Each axis has labels, title, ticks, and legends.
- `plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)`: Creates figure and grid of subplots.
- Plot types: Line (`plot`), Scatter (`scatter`), Bar (`bar`), Histogram (`hist`).

code_walkthroughs.title: Creating Figure and Line Plot Attributes
code_walkthroughs.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [10, 20, 30], label='Trend')
ax.set_title('Growth')
print('Title:', ax.get_title(), 'Lines:', len(ax.lines))
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Initializes an axis, plots a data series, sets title, and inspects figure properties programmatically.

practice_challenges.title: Chart Data Aggregator & Boundary Analysis
practice_challenges.description: Read a space-separated line of numbers representing monthly sensor readings. Calculate the 3-point moving average: `avg(i-1, i, i+1)` for `1 <= i <= len-2`. Print the moving averages rounded to 1 decimal place, space-separated.
practice_challenges.starter_code: # Compute 3-point moving average for chart series
practice_challenges.solution_code:
nums = [float(x) for x in input().split()]
ma = []
for i in range(1, len(nums) - 1):
    ma.append((nums[i-1] + nums[i] + nums[i+1]) / 3)
print(' '.join(f'{x:.1f}' for x in ma))

hints.level_1_nudge: Loop from index 1 to len(nums) - 2. Average the current, previous, and next numbers.
hints.level_2_strategy: Append (nums[i-1] + nums[i] + nums[i+1]) / 3, then format with f'{x:.1f}'.
hints.level_3_clue:

    ma.append((nums[i-1] + nums[i] + nums[i+1]) / 3)

sessions.title: Session 26 - Seaborn Statistical Graphics & Data Visualization

lessons.title: Statistical Distribution Analysis & Five-Number Summaries
lessons.concept_markdown:
Seaborn provides high-level APIs for statistical exploration:
- **Boxplots**: Visualizes the five-number summary: Minimum, Q1 (25th percentile), Median (50th percentile), Q3 (75th percentile), and Maximum, with dots representing outliers beyond `1.5 * IQR`.
- **IQR Formula**: `IQR = Q3 - Q1`.
- **Outliers**: Any value `< Q1 - 1.5 * IQR` or `> Q3 + 1.5 * IQR`.

code_walkthroughs.title: Computing Quartiles and IQR
code_walkthroughs.code:
import numpy as np
data = np.array([1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 100])
q1, q3 = np.percentile(data, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
print('Q1:', q1, 'Q3:', q3, 'IQR:', iqr)
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Calculates 25th and 75th percentiles and the interquartile range used in Seaborn boxplots.

practice_challenges.title: Boxplot Outlier Detector
practice_challenges.description: Read a space-separated line of numbers from input. Calculate the 25th percentile (`Q1`) and 75th percentile (`Q3`) using `np.percentile(arr, [25, 75])`. Compute `IQR = Q3 - Q1`. Count how many elements in the array are outliers (`value < Q1 - 1.5*IQR` or `value > Q3 + 1.5*IQR`). Print the count as integer.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import numpy as np

# Count outliers outside 1.5 * IQR
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([float(x) for x in input().split()])
q1, q3 = np.percentile(arr, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lower = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
outliers = ((arr < lower) | (arr > upper)).sum()
print(int(outliers))

hints.level_1_nudge: Compute q1, q3 = np.percentile(arr, [25, 75]) and iqr = q3 - q1.
hints.level_2_strategy: Thresholds are q1 - 1.5 * iqr and q3 + 1.5 * iqr. Count matches using boolean mask.

questions.title: Histogram Frequency Binning
questions.description: Read an integer `B` (number of bins). Then read a space-separated line of numbers. Using `np.histogram(arr, bins=B)`, compute the count of elements in each bin. Print the bin frequency counts space-separated.
questions.starter_code:
import numpy as np

b = int(input())
# Compute and print histogram bin frequencies
questions.solution_code:
import numpy as np

b = int(input())
arr = np.array([float(x) for x in input().split()])
counts, _ = np.histogram(arr, bins=b)
print(' '.join(map(str, counts)))

hints.level_2_strategy: np.histogram returns (counts, bin_edges). Join counts with spaces.
